title: NetworkError and stricter retries
summary: Ky now wraps fetch network failures in a typed NetworkError. It retries only errors it knows, and throws everything else at once.

links.title: Issue #545: Best way to handle fetch errors
PR #842: why the detector is inlined

steps.title: The problem
steps.body:
- Fetch rejects with a raw `TypeError` when the network fails.
- The message depends on the runtime. Chrome says `Failed to fetch`. Firefox says `NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.`
- Users could not tell a network failure from any other thrown error (#545).
- Before this PR, Ky retried every error that its timeout and HTTP status rules did not reject.
- Ky also retried programming bugs, because a bug is an unknown error too.

links.title: Issue #545: Best way to handle fetch errors
#545: Failed to fetch in the Instagram in-app browser

steps.title: The decision
steps.body:
- Ky wraps each recognized raw network error in a new `NetworkError`.
- By default, Ky retries only `HTTPError`, `TimeoutError` and `NetworkError`. It throws every other error at once.
- sholladay named the cost: a new runtime's unrecognized network error gets no retry. sindresorhus accepted it: "New runtimes don't come along every day."
- `shouldRetry` is the escape hatch for errors that the detector misses.
- Ky inlines the `is-network-error` v1.3.1 detector. Ky keeps zero runtime dependencies.

links.title: PR #842: why the detector is inlined

terms.meaning: The `KyError` subclass that Ky throws when fetch fails at the network level, for example on a DNS failure or a refused connection.
A `TypeError` from fetch whose message is on a known list of per-runtime network messages, such as `Failed to fetch` or `fetch failed`.
The public check that passes when the error is a `NetworkError` instance or has the name `NetworkError`.
The private method that returns the wait in ms before the next attempt, or throws the error to stop retrying.
The user option that overrides the default checks: `true` forces a retry, `false` stops, and `undefined` keeps the defaults.
The standard `Error` property where a `NetworkError` keeps the raw network error from fetch.
An HTTP method in `retry.methods` that Ky may retry, by default `get`, `put`, `head`, `delete`, `options` and `trace`.

steps.title: Parts of the retry path
steps.say: Every Ky attempt runs through `#fetch`. The PR wraps network failures there. It also adds a last check to the retry decision.

notes.text: `Ky.create` starts the first attempt through `#retry`. Every attempt goes through `#fetch`. Only `#fetch` calls `fetch`, the global one or a custom one from options.
When `fetch` rejects, `#fetch` asks `isRawNetworkError` about the error. On a match, `#fetch` throws a `NetworkError` with the original error as `cause`. `#fetch` rethrows any other error unchanged.

`#retry` hands each error to `#retryFromError`. `#retryFromError` asks the retry decision, `#calculateRetryDelay`, for a delay. `#retryFromError` waits for that delay, then calls `#retry` again. If the retry decision throws instead, no retry happens.

The retry decision keeps its earlier checks, such as the retriable method and `shouldRetry`. The PR adds a last check after them. An error that fails the `isNetworkError` guard there is thrown, not retried.
Apps import `NetworkError` and the `isNetworkError` guard from `ky`. The retry decision uses the same public guard.

steps.title: One network failure, then success
steps.say: A GET fails once with `TypeError('Failed to fetch')`, then succeeds. Ky wraps the failure and retries. The GET resolves with the second response.

messages.label: #fetch()
messages.note: `Ky.create` starts the first attempt of `ky.get(url)` here.

messages.label: TypeError: Failed to fetch
messages.note: `#fetch` catches the rejection. `isRawNetworkError` recognizes the message as a raw network error.

messages.label: #calculateRetryDelay(error)
messages.note: `#retry` passes the error through `#retryFromError` to the retry decision.

messages.label: delay (ms)
messages.note: GET is a retriable method. The `NetworkError` passes the `isNetworkError` guard, so the retry decision returns a backoff delay.

messages.label: #fetch()
messages.note: `#retryFromError` waits for the delay. It runs the `beforeRetry` hooks, then calls `#retry` again.

messages.label: 200 Response
messages.note: The `ky.get` promise resolves with this response. The first failure does not reject it.

steps.title: Check
steps.question: With default retry options, which failed first attempt does Ky now retry?

options.text: A GET where `fetch` rejects with `TypeError('Failed to fetch')`.
options.why: `#fetch` wraps the error in a `NetworkError`, and the retry decision retries a `NetworkError` on a GET.

options.text: A GET where `fetch` rejects with `TypeError('Cannot read properties of undefined')`.
options.why: `isRawNetworkError` does not match this message, so the error stays a `TypeError` and the last check throws it.

options.text: A POST where `fetch` rejects with `TypeError('Failed to fetch')`.
options.why: POST is not a retriable method by default, so the method check throws the `NetworkError` before the last check runs.

steps.title: A fetch failure becomes a NetworkError
steps.say: When `fetch` rejects, `#fetch` now passes the error to `isRawNetworkError`. A recognized network failure leaves `#fetch` as a `NetworkError`.

notes.text: With a timeout set (10 s by default), `#fetch` races `fetch` against `timeout()`. The call now sits inside the new `try` and uses `return await`. Without the `await`, a rejection would leave `#fetch` before the `catch` runs.

The `catch` passes each rejection to `isRawNetworkError`. On a match, it throws a `NetworkError` for `this.request`, with the raw error as `cause`. When `retry.limit` is above 0, `this.request` is the clone for the next attempt, not the object sent to `fetch`.
`isRawNetworkError` first requires a real `Error` named `TypeError` with a string message. The check uses `Object.prototype.toString`, not `instanceof`, so an error from another realm also passes.
Safari 17 and later use the generic message `Load failed`, with no stack. The check accepts `Load failed` only without a stack, or with the `__sentry_captured__` marker that Sentry adds.
Deno messages start with `error sending request for url`. Chrome sends `Failed to fetch`, or `Failed to fetch (host)` with the hostname in parentheses.

Line 48 matches every other message exactly against this set. The set covers Chrome, Firefox, Safari 16, `cross-fetch`, undici, Bun and Cloudflare Workers. The Bun entry starts with a space on purpose.

Like `TimeoutError`, `NetworkError` has a literal `name` and a `request`. Its message names the method and the URL. `KyError` has no constructor, so `{cause}` goes straight to the standard `Error` constructor.

The test sets `retry: 0` and makes `fetch` throw `TypeError('Failed to fetch')`. The error passes `instanceof NetworkError`, `isNetworkError` and `isKyError`. It keeps the raw `TypeError` as `cause` and has the message `Request failed due to a network error: GET https://example.com/`.

steps.title: Ky retries only known errors
steps.say: The retry decision keeps its early checks. Timeouts and retriable HTTP statuses now return their delay inside their own branches. A new last check retries a `NetworkError` and throws every other error.

notes.text: At the retry limit, the retry decision throws the error it got. For a network failure, that is now the last `NetworkError`. The `beforeError` hooks receive it, not the raw `TypeError`.
The `ForceRetryError` check and the retriable method check are unchanged.
`shouldRetry` runs next and is also unchanged. It now receives the `NetworkError`, because `#fetch` wraps the error before the retry decision runs.
A `TimeoutError` with `retryOnTimeout` on now returns its delay here. Without this `return`, the new last check would throw it.
When no `Retry-After` delay applies, a retriable HTTP status now returns its delay at line 482. The rules above it are unchanged.
This last check is new. Ky throws any error that fails `isNetworkError`, with no retry. Only a `NetworkError` reaches the default backoff at line 490.
Before, the `HTTPError` branch had no `return`. Retriable statuses, retried timeouts and every unknown error fell through to this shared `return`.
The last check calls the public `isNetworkError` guard. It passes on `instanceof NetworkError` or on the name `NetworkError`, like `isHTTPError` and `isTimeoutError`.
`isKyError` now also accepts what `isNetworkError` accepts. `instanceof KyError` already covered `NetworkError` instances, so this adds only the name match.
The test fails `fetch` twice with `TypeError('Failed to fetch')`, then returns `ok`. With `limit: 2`, Ky makes 3 calls and resolves with `ok`.

steps.title: Check
steps.question: What happens when `fetch` rejects with `TypeError('Failed to fetch')` on every call of a GET with `retry.limit` 2?

options.text: `fetch` runs 3 times, and `beforeError` gets a `NetworkError` with the `TypeError` as `cause`.
options.why: Ky wraps each failure, retries the `NetworkError` twice, and throws the last one at the limit.

options.text: `fetch` runs 3 times, and `beforeError` gets the raw `TypeError('Failed to fetch')`.
options.why: `#fetch` wraps the error before the retry decision runs, so the thrown error is a `NetworkError`.

options.text: `fetch` runs once, and `beforeError` gets a `NetworkError` with the `TypeError` as `cause`.
options.why: GET is a retriable method and a `NetworkError` passes the last check, so Ky retries it.

options.text: `fetch` runs 2 times, and `beforeError` gets a `NetworkError` with the `TypeError` as `cause`.
options.why: `limit` counts retries, not calls, so the first call plus 2 retries makes 3 calls.

steps.title: Ky throws a bug at once
steps.say: A `TypeError` from a bug is not a raw network error. Ky does not wrap it and does not retry it, even with retries left.

notes.text: `isRawNetworkError` does not match a message such as `Cannot read properties of undefined`. So the catch rethrows the `TypeError` unchanged, not as a `NetworkError`.

On a GET with retries left and no `shouldRetry`, the `TypeError` is not a `TimeoutError` or an `HTTPError`. So it reaches the last check. `isNetworkError` returns false, and the last check throws the `TypeError` on the first attempt.

The test sets `limit: 2` and a `fetch` that always throws the bug `TypeError`. `fetch` runs once, and the raw `TypeError` reaches the caller. Before this PR, Ky retried the same error up to the limit.

steps.title: shouldRetry can force a retry
steps.say: `shouldRetry` runs before the last check. When it returns `true`, Ky retries an error that the last check would throw. This is the escape hatch for errors that `isRawNetworkError` misses.

notes.text: Ky calls `shouldRetry` after the method check. It runs before the timeout, HTTP and `isNetworkError` checks. For a bug, `shouldRetry` gets the raw `TypeError`.
`true` returns a backoff delay at once. The error never reaches the last check, so the last check cannot stop this retry.

With `shouldRetry: () => true` and `limit: 2`, the bug `TypeError` makes `fetch` run 3 times. Then the limit check throws the raw `TypeError`, not a `KyError`. A caller that checks `isKyError` does not catch it.

steps.title: Ky does not retry a failed POST
steps.say: On a POST, `#fetch` still wraps a network failure in a `NetworkError`. The method check then throws it without a retry.

notes.text: The method check runs before `shouldRetry` and the last check. POST is not a retriable method by default, so the method check throws the `NetworkError`. `shouldRetry` does not run for it.

A POST with `limit: 2` and a `fetch` that throws `TypeError('Failed to fetch')` runs `fetch` once. The caller still gets a `NetworkError`, because `#fetch` wraps the error before the retry decision runs.

steps.title: Wrapping with the timeout disabled
steps.say: With `timeout: false`, `#fetch` calls `fetch` directly, without the `timeout()` helper. The PR adds `await` to that call. Network errors on this branch now become a `NetworkError` too.

notes.text: Before: this branch returned the `fetch` promise as is. That worked while `#fetch` had no `catch`.
Inside the `try`, the branch now uses `return await`. Without `await`, the rejection would skip the `catch`. Ky would then throw the raw `TypeError`.
The test turns off the timeout and makes `fetch` throw `TypeError('Failed to fetch')`. Ky still throws a `NetworkError` with the `TypeError` as `cause`. The test fails if the `await` goes away.

steps.title: undici client bugs become NetworkError
steps.say: undici, the `fetch` in Node.js, rejects with `TypeError('fetch failed')` for client bugs too. Ky wraps these errors as `NetworkError` and retries them on retriable methods. The readme says the opposite: Ky throws programming bugs at once.

notes.text: `fetch failed` is on the exact-match list. undici puts the real reason in the error's `cause`. `isRawNetworkError` never reads the `cause`.
The test sends a POST with the header `content-length: 0` and the body `sup`. undici rejects the mismatch with `fetch failed`.

Ky now throws a `NetworkError` for this client bug. The undici code moved one level deeper, to `error.cause.cause.code`. A PUT with the same mismatch would get retries, because PUT is a retriable method.

A POST to the URL `invalid:` fails in undici with `fetch failed`, because the scheme is unknown. The test now expects a `NetworkError`. It no longer checks the message `fetch failed`, because the message is now Ky's.

steps.title: Any error named NetworkError passes
steps.say: `isNetworkError` falls back to a name check, like the other Ky guards. So any error named `NetworkError` passes. The retry decision uses this guard, so it retries such an error on a retriable method.

notes.text: A browser `DOMException` named `NetworkError` passes, and so does an app's own class with that name. The type then claims a `request` property that these errors do not have. No test covers this case.

steps.title: Other errors Ky does not retry
steps.body:
- A thrown non-`Error` value, such as a string, is thrown at once. Before, Ky retried it.
- A user abort (`AbortError`) now stops at the retry decision. Before, it reached the backoff wait, and the wait rejected on the aborted signal.
- A custom `fetch` with its own error type, such as node-fetch `FetchError`, is not wrapped. By default, Ky does not retry it.
- An unlisted or localized runtime message stays a raw `TypeError` with no retry. So does a Safari `Load failed` error that has a stack.
- A network error while reading the body, such as undici `terminated` in `.json()`, happens after `#fetch` returns. Ky does not wrap it, so `isNetworkError` returns false.

steps.title: Check
steps.question: A node-fetch custom `fetch` rejects a GET with a `FetchError`: what happens by default, and what brings the retries back?

options.text: Ky throws the `FetchError` after 1 call. A `shouldRetry` that returns `true` for it restores retries.
options.why: `shouldRetry` runs before the last check, so `true` retries the unwrapped `FetchError`.

options.text: Ky wraps it in a `NetworkError` and retries it up to the limit. No change is needed.
options.why: `isRawNetworkError` requires the name `TypeError`, so Ky does not wrap a `FetchError`.

options.text: Ky throws the `FetchError` after 1 call. A `beforeRetry` hook that matches `FetchError` restores retries.
options.why: `beforeRetry` runs only after the retry decision returns a delay, so it never runs for this error.

options.text: Ky retries it up to the limit, then throws a `NetworkError` whose `cause` is the `FetchError`.
options.why: The last check throws every error that is not a `NetworkError`, so no retry happens.

steps.title: What to check
steps.body:
- A `catch` that checks `instanceof TypeError` now misses wrapped network failures. The `beforeRetry` workaround from #545 now stops network retries, because the `is-network-error` package accepts only errors named `TypeError`. The PR does not mark either change as breaking.
- When `isRawNetworkError` misses a network failure, Ky throws the error with no retry and no log. Check if `shouldRetry` is enough as the only escape hatch.
- The readme says Ky throws programming bugs at once. On Node, a `content-length` mismatch still becomes a `NetworkError`. Ky retries it on retriable methods.
- `isNetworkError` can give the wrong answer. It passes a `DOMException` named `NetworkError`, which has no `request`. It returns false for an undici `terminated` error during a body read, because Ky wraps only errors thrown inside `#fetch`.
- `NetworkError.message` holds the full URL, as the `HTTPError` and `TimeoutError` messages do. Tokens in the query string may reach logs.

steps.title: In short
steps.body:
- `#fetch` wraps a raw network error in a `NetworkError`. The raw `TypeError` moves to `error.cause`.
- The retry decision now retries only `NetworkError`, `TimeoutError`, `HTTPError` and `ForceRetryError`. It throws any other error at once, bugs included.
- The method check and `shouldRetry` still run before the new `isNetworkError` check. `shouldRetry` returning `true` still retries any error.
- `shouldRetry`, `beforeRetry` and `beforeError` now get the `NetworkError`. Check it with `isNetworkError`, not `instanceof TypeError`.
- `isRawNetworkError` matches a fixed list of runtime messages. Ky does not wrap or retry a network failure with an unlisted message.

steps.title: Also changed
steps.body:
- `readme.md` documents the new retry rules. It adds a `NetworkError` section with an `isNetworkError` example.
- Doc comments only: `source/errors/HTTPError.ts`, `source/errors/KyError.ts`, `source/types/hooks.ts`, `source/types/retry.ts`, `source/types/options.ts`. They name `NetworkError`, and they say `maxRetryAfter` caps the wait instead of cancelling the request.
- Imports and exports: `source/index.ts` exports `NetworkError` and `isNetworkError`. `source/core/Ky.ts`, `source/utils/type-guards.ts` and `test/memory-leak.ts` add the imports.
- `test/hooks.ts` fakes network failures with `TypeError('Failed to fetch')`, because Ky no longer retries the old messages by default. It asserts `isNetworkError` and renames one test.
- `test/retry.ts` adds more tests: a non-network `TypeError` stays unwrapped, `shouldRetry` gets the `NetworkError`, `undefined` from `shouldRetry` keeps the default retry, and `beforeError` sees the `cause`. The imports now span several lines.
